analysis.one_liner: Sets national patient protections for managed care, including emergency coverage, specialist access, external appeals, and the right to sue.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate vote; it sat on the Senate calendar until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set a list of enforceable rights for the roughly 150 million Americans with employer-based or other private health coverage, most of it then managed through HMOs and other managed care plans. Plans would have to cover emergency room visits without prior approval, let patients see specialists and OB-GYNs directly, disclose how their rules and financial incentives work, handle grievances quickly, and submit disputed denials to outside reviewers. Patients would also gain a new right to sue their health plan under federal law for injuries caused by wrongful denials of care. The bill was paid for in part by reinstating expired corporate environmental taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in group health plans and private health insurance, especially those in HMO-style plans with narrow networks: emergency care would be covered without prior authorization and without extra out-of-network charges [S2]; women could see an OB-GYN directly and children a pediatrician [S2]; patients with serious illnesses would get standing specialist referrals, continuity of care when a provider leaves the network, coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials, and access to non-formulary drugs when medically indicated [S2]; every plan would have to run a grievance system with internal and independent external appeals [S2]; and patients would regain the ability to sue plans in court for personal injury or wrongful death caused by wrongful denial of care, a right largely blocked since 1974 for most employer plans [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in managed care health plans

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency services without prior authorization, whether or not the provider is in-network, using a 'prudent layperson' standard, and patients cannot be billed more than they would owe an in-network provider.

Patients get direct access to obstetrician-gynecologists and pediatricians, standing referrals for ongoing conditions, continuity of care when a doctor leaves the network, and coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials.
Plans must run grievance systems with timely internal appeals and independent external appeals conducted by conflict-free entities, with binding decisions in as little as 72 hours for urgent cases.

The bill reverses part of a 1974 law (ERISA) so patients can sue under state law for personal injury or wrongful death caused by a plan's or insurer's wrongful denial of care, with lawsuits against employers limited to cases where the employer itself decided the claim.

Plans cannot gag doctors from discussing treatment options with patients, cannot pay reviewers based on the number of denials they issue, and must follow limits on financial incentives that reward withholding care.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans would bear the direct cost of new coverage mandates, faster decision deadlines, external appeals, and lawsuit exposure, which they would pass on as higher premiums; employers would likely see higher health benefit costs and typically pass some of that to workers in wages; chemical and waste-related industries would pay a reinstated corporate environmental tax and Superfund financing rate used to offset the bill's costs.

drawbacks.text: The requirements would raise the cost of insurance: new coverage mandates, rapid-decision deadlines, external review, and litigation risk all add expense, and employers would likely respond with higher premiums, higher employee cost-sharing, or fewer offers of coverage.

The bill itself concedes some of this cost-shifting: it lets plans charge higher premiums or cost-sharing for point-of-service options and does not require employers to pay any of the new costs, so employees could bear much of the burden.

The offsets are corporate taxes — a reinstated environmental tax and Superfund financing rate — whose burden ultimately falls partly on consumers and workers, and the liability expansion invites a wave of litigation whose costs are hard to predict.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address real, documented harms of 1990s managed care — denied emergency care, blocked specialists, secret financial incentives, and no meaningful recourse. The costs are genuine but were the standard trade-off the whole patients' bill of rights debate turned on: better protections mean somewhat higher premiums. As drafted, the bill was a broad, well-constructed version of the Democratic approach, though its liability expansion was the most contested element and a fair criticism is that it shifts costs onto workers through premiums.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the legislative calendar, but it was introduced less than three months before the Congress ended and the Senate never brought it to the floor for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle, for himself and Sen. Ted Kennedy, introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 1998 in the Senate on September 29, 1998.

The Senate read the bill a first time and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar on September 29, then read it a second time and placed it on the calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 683) on October 2, 1998.

No committee was assigned and no further action was taken; the bill remained on the calendar until the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so it never received a Senate vote and never reached the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans avoided the new coverage mandates, appeal rights, and lawsuit exposure, and employers avoided possible higher health benefit costs; patients in managed care got none of the proposed protections, which were not enacted until years later in weaker form.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 1998 in the Senate on September 29, 1998.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's cosponsor; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Kennedy'.

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it sat on the legislative calendar until the Congress ended, five weeks after it was introduced.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive patients' bill of rights legislation, particularly the right to sue health plans and the federal coverage mandates, lobbying Congress throughout 1998.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored by the two leading Senate Democrats and drew no Republican support in the record; the broader 1998 patients' bill of rights fight split largely on party lines, with the Senate's Democratic version failing on a near party-line procedural vote that summer.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill subjects every group health plan and insurer to binding coverage mandates, strict deadlines, independent external review of denials, and a new right to sue patients could use against them under state law. Their gain from the bill dying was continued freedom to manage care with limited recourse for patients.

Employers faced likely higher premiums from the mandates, but the bill largely shields them from lawsuits — suits against employers are allowed only when the employer itself decided the claim. They benefit from the bill's failure.
The bill's revenue title reinstates a corporate environmental tax and the Superfund hazardous substance financing rate to help pay for the patient protections. The tax lapsed when the bill died.

The bill bans contract 'gag clauses' restricting doctor-patient communication, requires prompt coverage decisions, bars retaliation against doctors who report quality problems, and curbs plan financial incentives that reward withholding care. It never took effect.
